sentences.text: The holotype skull of Nasutoceratops is approximately 1.5 meters long.
This dinosaur possessed three horns: one nasal horn located above the nasal opening and two brow horns situated above the eye sockets.
Nasutoceratops features a bulbous, almost circular snout that expands upwards, resembling the basal centrosaurine Diabloceratops rather than more advanced forms.
The skull frill of Nasutoceratops was almost circular, reaching its maximum width at the middle section.
The three frontmost neck vertebrae of Nasutoceratops were fused into a single syncervical vertebra, a structure particularly similar to that found in Styracosaurus.
Scott Sampson described the large nose of Nasutoceratops as a jumbo-sized schnoz in the museum's press release.
The unique hexagonal scale pattern on Nasutoceratops resembles star patterns later found on the limbs of Psittacosaurus.
Nasutoceratops possessed dental batteries with continuously replaced teeth adapted for processing large quantities of fibrous plants.
Rare patches of skin were preserved on the forelimb of a Nasutoceratops specimen, a finding uncommon for ceratopsians.
This is notable because pneumatic nasals are unknown in any other ceratopsian, supporting that this feature represents a unique derived trait of this genus.
The first known specimens of Nasutoceratops were discovered in the Kaiparowits Formation of the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in Utah starting in 2006.
Eric K. Lund discovered the holotype specimen of Nasutoceratops at locality VP 940 during the 2006 field season.
The species Nasutoceratops titusi was formally named in 2013, using a subadult skull as the holotype.
The skull shape of Nasutoceratops increased chewing efficiency by positioning the beak closer to the jaw joint.
In 2017, researchers proposed that different jaw mechanics allowed Nasutoceratops and other centrosaurines to coexist by reducing competition for food.
Coprolites attributed to Nasutoceratops contained angiosperm wood, indicating a diet of woody browse.
Coprolites from Nasutoceratops contained traces of mollusc shells, arthropod cuticle, and lizard bones alongside plant material.
In 2023, researchers suggested Nasutoceratops may have been solitary or rare in floodplain habitats based on finding only one specimen per quarry.
In 2017, Nicole Marie Ridgwell described coprolites possibly from Nasutoceratops in the Kaiparowits Formation.
Nasutoceratops is classified as a dinosaur in the order Ornithischia, family Ceratopsidae, and subfamily Centrosaurinae.
In 2013, researchers assigned Nasutoceratops to the subfamily Centrosaurinae based on specific skull features including a downward-angled premaxilla and a circular nostril region.
In 2018, the genus Crittendenceratops was described from Arizona and assigned to the clade Nasutoceratopsini.
Nasutoceratops was assigned to the Centrosaurinae in 2013 in a relatively basal position.
Nasutoceratops lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 76.0 to 75.5 million years ago.
Nasutoceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous epoch, specifically the Campanian stage, between 75.9 and 75.5 million years ago.
Nasutoceratops lived during the late Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous and coexisted with derived centrosaurines like Styracosaurus and Centrosaurus while retaining primitive features.
Nasutoceratops fossils are known from the Kaiparowits Formation in Utah, dating to the late Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous.

Nasutoceratops shared its paleoenvironment with theropods such as dromaeosaurids, the troodontid Talos sampsoni, ornithomimids like Ornithomimus velox, tyrannosaurids like Albertosaurus and Teratophoneus, armored ankylosaurids, the duck-billed dinosaurs Parasaurolophus cyrtocristatus and Gryposaurus monumentensis, the ceratopsids Utahceratops gettyi and Kosmoceratops richardsoni, and the oviraptorosaurian Hagryphus giganteus.
It is debated whether Laramidia was divided into separate dinosaur provinces with endemic species, a hypothesis based on the relationship between Nasutoceratops and other contemporaries.
In 2013, researchers suggested that Nasutoceratops supported the hypothesis of long-term separation between northern and southern dinosaur communities in Laramidia.
In 2013, Sampson and colleagues noted that the consensus on the function of ceratopsid skull ornamentation was use in intraspecific signaling and combat.
According to this study, the existence of Nasutoceratops would support the hypothesis of fauna separation between the north and south of Laramidia.
